title: The Perseid Meteor Shower Peaks This Week—Here's How to Watch
summary:
Every August, the night sky puts on a show that's been dazzling humans for centuries: the Perseid meteor shower. This year, the peak arrives on the night of August 12 into the early morning of August 13, 2026, and conditions couldn't be better. A new moon means darker skies, so those streaking lights will be easier to spot than usual.

So what exactly are you seeing? Meteors—often called "shooting stars"—are actually tiny fragments of dust and rock left behind by comets as they orbit the Sun. When Earth plows through these debris trails, the bits slam into our atmosphere at extreme speeds and burn up, creating brilliant streaks of light. The Perseids are named after the constellation Perseus because they appear to radiate from that part of the sky. But the real source is Comet Swift-Tuttle, a massive object about 16 miles (26 km) wide that orbits the Sun roughly once every 133 years. It last swung by Earth in 1992 and won't return until 2126.

During the peak, you could see anywhere from 50 to 100 meteors per hour. Some of these are "fireballs"—meteors as bright as Jupiter or Venus. NASA scientists say Swift-Tuttle's unusually large nucleus sheds hundreds of space rocks, many big enough to create these brilliant explosions.

To make the most of the event, find a dark, open area away from city lights. Leave your telescope and binoculars at home—the shower is best viewed with your own eyes. Give your eyes about 15 minutes to adjust to the dark, then be patient. And don't forget to make a wish; who knows, it might just come true!
why_it_matters: Tracking the Perseids shows how Earth's yearly journey around the Sun connects to ancient cosmic material, and it demonstrates that some of the best science is visible without expensive equipment.

background_read: Comet Swift-Tuttle (the parent body of the Perseid meteor shower) is a huge comet whose orbit brings it into the inner solar system about every 133 years.
The dust and rock it leaves behind form a broad debris stream that Earth crosses every August, producing the annual Perseids.
Meteor showers appear to radiate from one region because the meteors enter the atmosphere along roughly parallel paths.
Perseus (a constellation in the northern sky, named after a hero from Greek mythology) is the apparent origin point for this shower.
Because the 2026 peak coincides with a new moon, even fainter meteors are likely to be visible under dark rural skies.
NASA scientists also value such showers as natural laboratories for studying comet debris and Earth's atmosphere.

perspectives.perspective: People who live under heavy light pollution
perspectives.description: For them, the promise of 50 to 100 meteors per hour may be unrealistic because artificial light washes out all but the brightest fireballs, making the experience unequal.

perspectives.perspective: Scientists who study small solar-system bodies
perspectives.description: They view the Perseids as useful evidence of how comet debris spreads and burns up, which helps map the dust environment Earth travels through.
Because Comet Swift-Tuttle will not return until 2126, protecting dark skies and teaching younger people to observe now is a way to keep the connection to this long-cycle event alive.
